items.stem: Internal (organic) growth occurs when a firm
options: expands by investing in new capacity and increasing its own sales
items.answer: expands by investing in new capacity and increasing its own sales
items.markingKey: Organic growth: reinvested profit, new plants, new products, new markets.

items.stem: Explain two advantages of internal growth compared with growth by merger.
items.answer: Lower risk and cost (no premium paid for another firm); no culture clash; growth can be controlled; avoids competition authority investigation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why a firm might choose conglomerate integration.
items.answer: To spread risk across unrelated markets, use spare managerial or financial capacity, or grow when its own market is saturated or tightly regulated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: diversification/risk; 1 mark: second reason [2]

items.stem: Cobalt Group, a firm in cheese making, takes over Everline, a firm in cheese making. Which type of integration is this?
items.answer: Horizontal integration
items.markingKey: Production chain: dairy farming → cheese making → supermarkets. Horizontal integration.

items.stem: Pinnacle plc, a firm in clothing retailing, takes over Everline, a firm in clothing retailing. Which type of integration is this?
items.answer: Horizontal integration
items.markingKey: Production chain: cotton farming → textile manufacturing → clothing retailing. Horizontal integration.

items.stem: Extract: Lumen Ltd (28% market share) has agreed to take over Ironleaf (20% share), a rival in the mobile telecommunications industry of Korvia. The firms claim savings of 8% on average costs. (a) Calculate the rise in the HHI caused by the merger. (b) Explain why the expected cost savings might not happen.
items.answer: (a) 2 × 28 × 20 = 1120 (b) Culture clash, diseconomies of scale, integration costs, loss of staff.

items.stem: A merger between two firms at the same stage of production in the same industry is
items.answer: horizontal integration
items.markingKey: Same industry, same stage: e.g. two banks.

items.stem: Distinguish between backward and forward vertical integration.
items.answer: Backward: a firm takes over a supplier at an earlier stage of production; forward: it takes over a firm at a later stage, closer to the consumer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a firm might choose conglomerate integration. (b) Distinguish between backward and forward vertical integration.

(b) Backward: a firm takes over a supplier at an earlier stage of production; forward: it takes over a firm at a later stage, closer to the consumer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: diversification/risk; 1 mark: second reason [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Keystone plc and Pinnacle plc, two firms in chocolate manufacturing, plan to merge. Identify the type of integration and analyse two benefits and one risk for the firm.
items.answer: Horizontal integration. Benefits: economies of scale, larger market share and pricing power, removal of duplication. Risks: diseconomies, culture clash, competition authority investigation, higher prices for consumers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: type; 2 marks: two benefits analysed; 1 mark: risk [4]

items.stem: Apex Ltd, a textile manufacturing business, plans to buy Everline, a chain in clothing retailing. Identify the type of integration and analyse two benefits and one risk for the firm.
items.answer: Forward vertical integration. Benefits: secure outlets, control of branding and pricing, capture retail margin, information on consumers. Risks: retail expertise needed, rival suppliers may lose access, high cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: type; 2 marks: two benefits analysed; 1 mark: risk [4]

items.stem: Meridian Group, a banking business, wants to double in size within five years. (a) Explain the ways in which a firm can grow internally. (b) Assess whether internal growth is better than external growth for a firm.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Internal growth is lower risk, retains culture and control. (b) Case for the view: Internal growth is lower risk, retains culture and control. Case against / evaluation: Slower; external growth is quicker, gains market share, brands and know-how; depends on finance and market conditions. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.

(b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: An acquisition (takeover) differs from a merger because
options: one firm buys a controlling share in another, rather than two firms agreeing to combine
it always involves firms in different countries

items.stem: Explain two reasons why many mergers fail to achieve the expected benefits.
items.answer: Culture clashes between workforces and managers; diseconomies of scale; overpaying for the target; synergies overestimated; loss of key staff and customers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain how a merger might benefit consumers.
items.answer: Cost savings from economies of scale passed on as lower prices; more funds for R&D and better products; a stronger competitor against a dominant firm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point developed [2]

items.stem: Market shares in the mobile telecommunications industry: Tidewater plc 26%, Cobalt Group 24%, Quarry Bay Ltd 15%, Horizon Corp 8%, Orchid Ltd 7%, and 10 small firms with 2% each. Tidewater plc proposes to merge with Orchid Ltd. Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio before the merger.

Market shares in the steel industry: Granite Holdings 25%, Horizon Corp 23%, Juniper Brands 16%, Pinnacle plc 13%, Delta Foods 7%, and 10 small firms with 1.6% each. Horizon Corp proposes to merge with Pinnacle plc. Calculate the HHI before and after the merger and the four-firm concentration ratio after the merger. Competition authorities investigate mergers that raise the HHI by more than 200 in a market with an HHI above 2,500. State, with a reason, whether this merger is likely to be investigated.
items.answer: HHI before = 1653.6; after = 2251.6 (rise of 598); CR4 after = 84%. Probably not investigated on these thresholds, because the post-merger HHI is below 2,500.
items.markingKey: HHI = Σs² = 1653.6 [1]; merged share 36%, so rise = 2 × 23 × 13 = 598 [1]; new HHI 2251.6 [1]; CR4 after 84% [1]; threshold applied [1].

They serve niche markets that are too small for large firms
They benefit from greater economies of scale

economies of scale are very large

items.answer: operate independently while using an established brand and support of a larger firm
items.markingKey: Franchisee gains brand, training and bulk-buying; franchisor gains fees.

items.stem: Meridian Group buys components from many small suppliers in Loristan rather than making them itself. Explain why this helps small firms survive.
items.answer: Subcontracting gives small firms a steady market and lets them specialise in a narrow activity where economies of scale are small; the large firm gains flexibility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: guaranteed demand/specialisation; 1 mark: link to survival [2]

items.stem: A family-run printed newspapers business in Lisbon has survived for 40 years despite competition from Everline, a national chain. Explain two reasons why it may have survived.
items.answer: It may serve a local niche with personal service and specialist knowledge, and be flexible in adapting to customer needs; low overheads and loyal customers help; the MES may be small.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason, 1 mark each developed [4]

items.stem: In Esteria, small firms make up 95% of the 4,000 businesses, employ 50% of workers and produce 42% of output. Explain why small firms may have lower labour productivity than large firms.
items.answer: Less capital per worker, fewer economies of scale, less specialisation and less access to finance and technology.

items.stem: In Halvoria, most businesses employ fewer than ten people. Discuss whether small firms will eventually disappear as large firms gain economies of scale.
items.answer: Arguments for: Large firms have cost advantages and market power. Arguments against / evaluation: Niche markets, small MES, flexibility, personal service, franchising, technology lowering entry costs, government support. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.
